result:
**Claim:** Yes. Every standard-open set is K-open.

**Setup.** The K-topology on ℝ has basis consisting of all open intervals (a,b) together with all sets (a,b) \ K, where K = {1/n : n ∈ ℕ, n ≥ 1}. The standard topology has basis consisting of the open intervals (a,b).

**Proof.** Let U be open in the standard topology and let x ∈ U. By the definition of the standard topology, there are a, b with x ∈ (a,b) ⊆ U. The interval (a,b) is itself a basis element of the K-topology. So every point of U lies in a K-basis element contained in U, and therefore U is a union of K-basis elements. Hence U is open in the K-topology. ∎

The same argument shows that the K-topology is finer than the standard topology. The reverse inclusion fails. The set ℝ \ K is K-open, being (−∞,∞) \ K, a union of basis elements (−n,n) \ K. But it is not standard-open, because 0 ∈ ℝ \ K and every interval around 0 contains some 1/n ∈ K. This does not affect the question asked.

Final answer: Yes, every standard-open set in ℝ is open in the K-topology (the K-topology is strictly finer).
